passage:
On the crowded bus back from the kasba school, Mehak's friends argued about the Sunday fair. "Let's skip the rides," said Bindu. "Yes, skip them," Mehak agreed, though she had been saving for the giant wheel. When Bindu frowned at her bag bumping someone, Mehak said sorry three times. When the group mocked a new girl's accent, Mehak laughed along, her stomach tight. Things stayed smooth. Nobody was ever cross with her.
Joseph, who sat behind her, leaned forward at her stop. "You love the giant wheel. Why didn't you say?"
Mehak opened her mouth and found nothing there. At home she lay on the charpai, trying to remember the last time she had said what she really thought, and she couldn't.

qa.q: What had Mehak been saving for?
qa.a: Mehak had been saving for the giant wheel.

qa.q: What was Mehak feeling when she laughed along at the new girl's accent?
qa.a: Mehak felt uneasy and tense; her stomach was tight even as she laughed to keep things smooth.

qa.q: What small step could Mehak try next time her friends make plans?
qa.a: Mehak could share one small real wish, like riding the giant wheel, to practise speaking up when little is at stake.

qa.q: How does Joseph see Mehak's quick agreement?
qa.a: Joseph notices that it does not match what Mehak really loves, and gently asks why she stayed quiet.

grounding: A teenager agrees, apologises and hides opinions to keep her friends calm, which keeps things smooth but leaves her unsure what she thinks.

passage:
Zeynep's father came up from the family bakery in Izmir tired and short-tempered most evenings, and fourteen-year-old Zeynep had become very good at keeping the air calm. She said, "Yes, Baba, sorry, Baba," before he finished a sentence, even when she hadn't done anything. When he asked whether she'd pick science next year, she said, "Whatever you think is best," though her sketchbooks filled a whole drawer.
Her cousin Emil, visiting from Berlin, watched her apologise for the rain. "Do you ever disagree with anyone?" he asked.
Zeynep laughed, then stopped. "I don't actually know what I'd say."
That night she wrote one sentence in her sketchbook: I want to choose art. It was small. But it was hers.

qa.q: What did Zeynep write in her sketchbook that night?
qa.a: Zeynep wrote: I want to choose art.

qa.q: What does Zeynep's answer "I don't actually know what I'd say" reveal about how she feels?
qa.a: It reveals Zeynep feels lost and unsettled, realising that keeping the peace has left her unsure of her own views.

qa.q: Why was writing one sentence a useful first step for Zeynep?
qa.a: Writing it privately let Zeynep name a real wish safely, a small start toward saying her opinions aloud.

qa.q: How does Emil see Zeynep's constant apologising?
qa.a: Emil finds it odd, since she even apologised for the rain, and wonders whether she ever disagrees.

grounding: A teenager agrees and apologises to keep home calm, then notices that it has quietly worn away her sense of what she wants.

passage: 'Sorry, sorry, you're right,' Gopika said, before Tenzin had even finished. They were at Tenzin's dining table in Jayanagar, building their chemistry project, and Tenzin had just rewritten Gopika's section for the third time. Gopika had liked her version. She said nothing about it. At home that evening, when her mother asked whether she wanted rice or chapati, she said, 'Whatever's easier, Amma. Sorry.' When her younger brother changed the TV channel, she smiled and gave him the remote. Later Tenzin texted: 'Be honest, which intro do you prefer?' Gopika stared at the screen for a long time. She honestly did not know any more. Every answer she started began with what Tenzin might want to hear. She typed 'Yours is great!' and then, slowly, deleted it. 'I think I liked my first one,' she wrote, her heart thudding.

qa.q: How many times had Tenzin rewritten Gopika's section?
qa.a: For the third time.

qa.q: What was Gopika feeling as she stared at Tenzin's text?
qa.a: She felt lost and anxious, unsure what she really thought because every answer began with what Tenzin might want.

qa.q: What small step did Gopika take, and why does it matter?
qa.a: She deleted 'Yours is great!' and wrote that she liked her first intro, a small honest opinion that begins rebuilding her own voice.

qa.q: How might Tenzin see Gopika's constant agreeing?
qa.a: Tenzin may think Gopika really agrees, and so never learns that her ideas are being lost.

grounding: Shows a teenager who apologises and agrees at home and with a friend to avoid friction, keeping things smooth at the cost of knowing her own opinions.

passage:
'Which film, Santosh?'
'Whatever you want. Sorry.'
'Why are you sorry? I asked you.'
'Sorry. I mean, anything's fine.'
Sahil stopped walking. 'That's nine sorries today. I counted. You didn't even want to come to cricket, but you said yes.'
Santosh laughed awkwardly. 'It's easier. At home, when Papa's had a bad day, the whole house goes tight. If I agree with everyone, it stays calm.'
'And here? We're not your Papa.'
'I know. I just... do it everywhere now.'
'Do you even know which film you want?'
Santosh was quiet. 'Honestly? Not really. Sometimes I don't know what I like any more.'
'Then practise on me. Pick. I won't be upset.'
A long pause. 'The space one.'
'See? Nothing exploded.'

qa.q: How many sorries had Sahil counted?
qa.a: Nine sorries today.

qa.q: Why does Santosh keep agreeing, and what does Santosh feel underneath?
qa.a: Santosh is anxious about tension and wants things to stay calm, and it leaves Santosh feeling lost about what to like.

qa.q: What could Santosh try next, building on this conversation?
qa.a: Santosh could keep practising small honest choices with safe friends like Sahil, such as picking a film or saying no to cricket.

qa.q: How is Sahil affected by Santosh's constant agreeing?
qa.a: Sahil feels puzzled and a little shut out, because Sahil wants a friend's real opinion, not an apology.

grounding: Shows a teenager who agrees quickly and says sorry constantly to keep peace at home and with friends, and how it leaves the teen unsure of their own likes.

passage: Looking back, I think I spent most of Class 11 saying yes. Yes to the science stream because everyone said I was good at maths. Yes to the group's plans, the group's jokes, the group's opinion of whoever was not there. If anyone frowned, I apologised, even when I had done nothing. It kept things smooth, and I was proud of being the easy one. Then, at a college fair, a volunteer asked what I actually enjoyed. My mind went empty. My friend Vinita, standing beside me, said quietly, 'You always ask what we think, Nitin. I don't think I've ever heard what you think.' That stung, because it was true. These days I practise small things: choosing where we eat, saying I didn't like a film. My voice shakes sometimes. But I'm slowly finding out who I am.

qa.q: What stream did Nitin say yes to?
qa.a: The science stream.

qa.q: What did Nitin feel when Vinita spoke at the college fair?
qa.a: Nitin felt stung and exposed, because it was true that nobody had heard Nitin's own opinion.

qa.q: What small steps is Nitin taking now?
qa.a: Nitin practises choosing where they eat and saying when a film was not good, even with a shaky voice.

qa.q: How might Vinita have experienced Nitin as a friend during Class 11?
qa.a: Vinita may have found Nitin easy to be with but hard to really know, since Nitin kept every opinion hidden.

grounding: Shows a teenager who agreed and apologised to keep peace, found it kept things smooth but left no sense of self, and begins to recover it.

passage:
School counsellor's note, Jasleen, Class 10
Jasleen was referred because she 'never causes any trouble.' In our first session she apologised four times: for being early, for her handwriting, for sitting in the wrong chair. When I asked what she thinks of her group choosing a project topic she dislikes, she said, 'Whatever they want is fine,' then went quiet. She told me she agrees with everyone quickly because arguments make her stomach knot, and that she no longer knows what she actually likes. Keeping everyone happy keeps things calm, but she seems to be disappearing. We practised one small step: saying 'I'd prefer...' once this week. She will try it with her group on Friday.
Tanuja

qa.q: How many times did Jasleen apologise in the first session?
qa.a: Four times.

qa.q: What does Jasleen feel when arguments happen?
qa.a: She feels anxious, her stomach knotting, so she agrees quickly to avoid conflict.

qa.q: What small step did Jasleen and Tanuja practise?
qa.a: Saying 'I'd prefer...' once this week, starting with her group on Friday.

qa.q: How might Jasleen's group see her?
qa.a: The group probably sees Jasleen as easy-going and agreeable, not noticing she hides her real opinions.

grounding: A teenager who agrees quickly and apologises constantly to avoid conflict keeps things calm but slowly loses her sense of self.
